hul_equiano.text: Wilberforce spoke in Parliament, but he didn't do it alone. Thomas Clarkson rode thousands of miles gathering evidence. Quakers started the first petitions.
And Olaudah Equiano, who had been enslaved as a boy, bought his freedom and wrote his life story in 1789. Thousands read it. People who had suffered spoke up loudest of all.

hul_medallion.text: Look at this little medallion: a kneeling man in chains, and the words 'Am I not a man and a brother?'. Josiah Wedgwood made them in 1787 and supporters wore them as brooches and hairpins.
Like a campaign badge. Two hundred years before badges.

then.text: Your petition's framed in the back office. Three names, and yours. That's how it was done: one signature at a time.
All three! The fisherman's widow, the Wolds churchwarden and even that clerk. Wonderful.
In 1792 more than five hundred petitions against the slave trade reached Parliament, the most ever sent on a single subject at the time. Ordinary people, writing their names, changed the law.
Please, take this. It was pressed in an old hymn book from the Minster, for luck.
Two names! Now for the hard one: the Parliamentary Clerk in Hull Minster says the form is wrong. Persuade him, firmly.
One name down. Next, out to the Wolds: the churchwarden at Rudston, by the great stone.

else.text: Start on Hessle Road. The fishing families knew all about hard lives. Ask in the terrace.
Welcome to Wilberforce House. William Wilberforce was born here in 1759, son of a Hull merchant.

He was elected MP for Hull at twenty-one, then for all Yorkshire. From 1787 he led the campaign in Parliament to end the slave trade: British ships had carried millions of enslaved Africans across the Atlantic.
The campaign worked because ordinary people joined it: they boycotted slave-grown sugar and signed petitions in their thousands.
Help gather names for a petition, as they did then?

then.text: Bless you. Three names: Hessle Road first, then Rudston on the Wolds, then that stubborn clerk at the Minster.

else.text: Another time. The house isn't going anywhere. It's been here since the 1660s.
